chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Yaqoub ibn Yazeed, from Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Nawfaly, raised it to Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) passed by a camel shepherd, so he sent to him to quench him, but he said, 'As for what is in their udders, it is for the morning, and as for what is in our containers, it is for the evening.' So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'O Allah! Increase his wealth and his children.'

Then he passed by a sheep shepherd, so he sent for him to quench him. So he milked for him whatever was in its udders, and poured what was in his container into the container of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), and sent a sheep to him, saying: 'This is what is with us, and if you love that we increase it for you, we will increase it for you.' He said, so the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'O Allah! Grant him sufficiency (al-kafaf).'

One of his companions said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah! You supplicated for the one who repulsed you with a supplication which the majority of us love, and you supplicated for the one who relieved you of your need with a supplication which we all dislike.' So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Indeed, what is little and sufficient is better than what is abundant and diverting. O Allah! Grant Muhammad and the Progeny of Muhammad sufficiency (al-kafaf).'

key_terms.الكَفَاف: sufficiency, moderate provision, enough to meet needs without excess

ai.seo_question: What is the meaning of 'al-kafaf' in the hadith of the two shepherds?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the Prophetic wisdom in distinguishing between material abundance and spiritual sufficiency, a key theme in Shia ethics regarding *al-Kafaf* (moderate provision). The Prophet’s specific prayer for the generous shepherd to have 'enough' rather than 'more' reflects the belief that excessive wealth can become a distraction (*lahw*) from divine remembrance, a nuance highlighted by the companion's query. This narrative underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on contentment and the spiritual dangers of accumulation, linking material state directly to spiritual focus.
